title: Consolidate 5 pending changes to backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py
design:
FILED BY THE ENG HEAD, NOT BY A HUMAN. 5 open changes all
conflict on the same file. Each was specified independently and each is
individually reasonable; together they are one piece of work, and landing them
one at a time costs 5 rebase-and-resolve cycles that each re-derive the
same integration.

TARGET FILE: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py

SOURCE CHANGES:
  - PABLO-o42 (PR #641, branch work/skip-refuted-checks): feat(pentest): add a persistent hypothesis ledger across runs
  - PABLO-ct2 (PR #642, branch work/report-cli-endpoint-bypass): Confirm the managed LLM endpoint before the pentest narrative call
  - PABLO-c2u (PR #643, branch work/narrative-gen-fallback): Fall back to the alternate LLM CLI before giving up on the narrative
  - PABLO-dns (PR #644, branch work/vary-retry-param): Vary sampling and escalate to an alternate model on pentest narrative retries
  - PABLO-o5m (PR #646, branch work/cross-tenant-probe): Run the cross-tenant IDOR probe as a deterministic collector

WHAT TO BUILD. One branch and one PR that satisfies EVERY acceptance block
below. Read all 5 source designs first — they are reproduced in full at the
end — and look for the shared structure before writing anything. Where the file
resists all of them for the same reason, fix that reason; a consolidation whose
only content is 5 changes stacked in one diff has done the mechanical half and
skipped the valuable half.

WHAT NOT TO DO:
  - Do NOT start from any of the existing branches. This is a new branch off
    main. The existing PRs stay open and untouched; they are closed by a human
    once this lands, and reading them is allowed but inheriting them is not.
  - Do NOT drop, defer, or "simplify away" any acceptance block. If one of them
    genuinely cannot coexist with another, that is a real finding: STOP, print
    WORKER-BLOCKED with the two blocks and why they conflict, and open no PR.
    A conflict between two specs is a decision for a human, not a tiebreak for
    a worker.
  - Do NOT change behaviour the acceptance blocks do not ask you to change. The
    existing test suite for this file is the invariant: every test that passed
    before must pass after.

HOW THIS IS CHECKED. A separate reviewer, which sees ONLY the final diff and the
acceptance blocks — not this design, not your commits, not your reasoning — will
answer each block with satisfied / not satisfied / cannot tell. Anything other
than satisfied blocks the merge and names the block that went missing. Write the
diff so that a reader with no context can find each block satisfied in it.

SOURCE DESIGNS, IN FULL:

--- PABLO-o42: feat(pentest): add a persistent hypothesis ledger across runs ---
Store alongside the evidence bundle and persist to the same reports bucket so the ledger survives between runs; read the last N (start with 8) at prompt-build time. Record the chain sketch in the same anchored form the design doc already requires — expressible as a sequence of HTTP requests, SQL queries or cloud API calls against the deployed system — so an entry is checkable rather than a vibe. Out of scope: acting on ledger entries automatically, and any change to how findings are reported.

--- PABLO-ct2: Confirm the managed LLM endpoint before the pentest narrative call ---
Make the routing explicit rather than incidental. Options in preference order: (1) assert it — before invoking, resolve which endpoint the CLI will use and fail closed if it is not the managed one; (2) record it — write the resolved endpoint and auth mode into the report's attestation block so every archived report states where the text came from; (3) remove the ambiguity — call the managed endpoint directly for the narrative step instead of shelling out to a CLI whose auth precedence is not ours to control. (3) composes well with splitting deterministic synthesis from agentic exploration. Touch points: _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude / _run_cli (~541-590), the attestation block in _assemble_report.

--- PABLO-c2u: Fall back to the alternate LLM CLI before giving up on the narrative ---
Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py — _invoke_llm (~line 410), the retry wrapper at ~466-500, the NARRATIVE GENERATION FAILED block at ~520, and run()/sys.exit at ~777. _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS (3000) stays the heuristic. Keep the existing narrative-failed report block verbatim; this bead changes control flow and exit status only. Out of scope: changing the prompt text (tracked on the collector bead), changing the format-failure threshold, provisioning the alternate model's entitlement.

--- PABLO-dns: Vary sampling and escalate to an alternate model on pentest narrative retries ---
Touch points: _invoke_llm (~410), the retry wrapper (~466-500), _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude (~541-572). The gemini CLI takes generation settings via its own flags/config — check what 0.38.x exposes before assuming temperature is reachable; if it is not, escalate straight to the model/provider ladder. Keep _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS as the failure heuristic. Order: attempt 1 default -> attempt 2 reinforced + varied sampling -> attempt 3 alternate model -> fail. Composes with PABLO-c2u (nonzero exit + alternate chaining); land that first if they are worked separately.

--- PABLO-o5m: Run the cross-tenant IDOR probe as a deterministic collector ---
Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_collectors.py (new collector, mirror the shape of the existing collectors and their bundle-summary entries), backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py::_build_prompt STEP 4 and STEP 5 (lines ~370-395). The two ephemeral identities are already provisioned by backend/app/jobs/pentest_identity.py and reach the prompt as PENTEST_TEST_ID_TOKEN_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_EMAIL_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_UID_A/B — the collector reads the same values. Severity classification for a FAIL stays where it already lives (backend/app/jobs/pentest_severity.py); the collector reports the observation, not the tier. Out of scope: adding new probe classes (intra-tenant IDOR is tracked separately), changing which scanners run, any IAM or infrastructure change.
acceptance_criteria:
Every block below must be satisfied by the single resulting diff. They are reproduced verbatim from the 5 source beads; they are numbered so the reviewer can answer each one separately.

title: [bug] test_update_status_to_discontinued_sets_stopped_at fails on any branch between 8pm and midnight US Eastern
design:
FOUND 2026-08-02 22:58 ET while running an unrelated frontend-only change
through `make check`.

backend/tests/test_routes_medications.py:224 compares a stopped_at value the
server derives in UTC against a locally computed date.today(). Between 20:00 and
23:59 US Eastern the UTC calendar date has already rolled over to tomorrow while
the local date has not, so the two disagree and the test fails. It passes at
every other hour, on every branch, with no code change involved.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FLAKE. It is not random - it is a
deterministic function of wall-clock time, so it cannot be reproduced by
re-running in the morning and looks like "the branch broke it" to whoever hits
it. And `make check` is a stated acceptance criterion on a large number of
beads, so during that four-hour window EVERY such bead has an unsatisfiable
acceptance criterion. An automated worker that hits it has no way to know the
failure is pre-existing and unrelated: it either burns its remaining budget
investigating backend code it never touched, or it declines to push work that
was actually complete. Both look like worker failure and neither is.

FIX: make the assertion timezone-honest rather than time-of-day dependent -
compare against the same UTC-derived date the server used (or freeze time).
Do not "fix" it by widening the assertion to accept either date; that hides
a real timezone bug class if one ever appears.

WORTH A SWEEP: this is unlikely to be the only test comparing a server UTC
value to a local date.today() / datetime.now(). Grep the suite for naive
date.today() and datetime.now() in assertions while you are in here.
acceptance_criteria:
- The test passes at any hour. Prove it by running the suite with the clock
  (or TZ) set into the 20:00-23:59 US Eastern window, not just by re-running it
  at a convenient time.
- Any sibling assertions comparing a server-side UTC value against a naive local
  date/time are found and fixed or explicitly ruled out.
- `make check` passes at the repo root.

title: Enforce availability rules on the appointment write path — HARD refuses, SOFT warns
design:
AVAILABILITY RULES ARE ADVISORY. The engine evaluates all eight rule types
correctly and has 34 passing tests, but it is wired into TWO read-only routes
and nothing else. A booking at 3am on a blocked day returns 201.

PROVEN 2026-08-02:
  - AvailabilityEngine is constructed in one factory
    (backend/app/routes/scheduling.py:150) and injected into exactly two routes,
    both read-only:
        :551  GET  /api/availability/slots
        :568  POST /api/availability/check
  - The write path never touches it: routes/scheduling.py:193 create_appointment
    -> scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42, which validates only
    patient_id / start_at / end_at / duration_minutes.
  - EnforcementLevel (HARD | SOFT) is defined at
    scheduling_engine/models/availability.py:24 and READ in exactly one
    expression in production code: routes/scheduling.py:584,
    `has_hard = any(c.enforcement == EnforcementLevel.HARD ...)`, which only
    shapes the response body of the check route. Nothing acts on it. The engine
    itself never inspects enforcement - it copies it onto the Conflict and moves
    on.
  - No frontend code calls /api/availability/* at all. The read path has no
    consumer today.

THE TELL: a two-level enforcement enum that no code enforces is a design that
anticipated a step nobody built. HARD vs SOFT is meaningless until something
refuses.

DEPENDS ON the double-booking bead. Both change the same functions
(create_appointment / update_appointment); landing them in parallel guarantees a
conflict. Collisions first (physics), then rules (policy).

SCOPE:
  1. Give SchedulingService access to AvailabilityEngine. The engine's
     constructor already takes (rule_repo, appointment_repo)
     - services/availability.py:40 - and the factory at routes/scheduling.py:150
     shows the DI shape. Keep SchedulingService constructible with just the repo
     so the ~35 existing tests that do SchedulingService(repo) keep compiling:
     an optional availability_engine parameter defaulting to None, with rule
     checking skipped when it is absent.
  2. On create, and on update when a time field changes, call
     engine.check_conflicts(user_id, start_at, end_at) - signature at
     services/availability.py:48, returns list[Conflict].
  3. Partition the result by conflict.enforcement:
       HARD -> refuse. Raise a rule-violation error mapped to HTTP 422, with
               every violated rule's message in the body. 422 distinguishes
               "you may not book this" from the 409 the collision bead returns
               for "something is already there" - two different fixes for the
               user, so two different codes.
       SOFT -> allow, and return the warnings alongside the created
               appointment so the caller can surface them. A SOFT rule that
               silently vanishes is the same bug in a smaller box.
  4. Identity: the write routes use user.id (from require_baa_acceptance) while
     the availability routes use ctx.user_id (TenantContext). Same value in
     practice today. Pick one deliberately and be consistent - the engine's
     methods are written against ctx.user_id.

KNOWN SHARP EDGES, worth handling or explicitly deferring in the notes:
  - rule.params is an untyped dict with NO validation at any layer
    (models/availability.py:40); the create-rule route passes it through raw
    (:631). Malformed params surface as a KeyError from inside the engine
    (e.g. availability.py:154). Once rules gate writes, a bad rule stops being a
    cosmetic problem and starts refusing legitimate bookings. Either validate
    params per rule type, or catch and treat an unevaluable rule as
    non-blocking - do NOT let a KeyError become a 500 on the booking path.
  - Buffer minutes are wall-clock and same-day clamped
    (availability.py:375-391), so an appointment crossing midnight is silently
    truncated. Note it; fixing it is not this bead.

OUT OF SCOPE: overlap detection (the dependency owns it), UI, and any
per-clinician policy table.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A booking that violates a HARD rule (blocked day, outside working hours) is
   refused with 422 and a body naming the violated rule; the appointment is not
   created.
2. A booking that violates only a SOFT rule succeeds and returns the warnings.
3. A booking that violates nothing still succeeds.
4. A user with no rules is unaffected.
5. The same enforcement applies to PATCH when a time field changes, and the
   start-session internal update still does not trip it.
6. A malformed rule (params missing an expected key) does not 500 the booking
   path - covered by a test.
7. Tests call POST /api/appointments through the route, not just the service.
8. `make check` passes at the repo root.
notes:
Paths verified present on main 2026-08-16: backend/app/routes/scheduling.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/models/availability.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py.

Sequencing note: this and the double-booking refusal both edit the scheduling route and service. They are complementary, not duplicates — one enforces the therapist's availability rules, the other rejects overlaps — but they touch the same two files, so they must not be worked simultaneously. Whichever starts first should land before the other begins; the second will need to rebase on it.

title: Add an overlap query to the appointment repository — list_overlapping on the ABC and both implementations
design:
THE MISSING PRIMITIVE. Nothing in the appointment repository can answer "does
this proposed time collide with an existing appointment?", which is why the
write path cannot check for double-booking even though it obviously should.
This bead adds ONLY that primitive plus its tests. No route changes, no service
changes - those follow in a separate bead so this one lands small and green.

WHY list_by_range IS NOT IT (verified 2026-08-02):
  backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py:85-87 filters
      AppointmentRow.user_id == user_id
      AppointmentRow.start_at >= start
      AppointmentRow.start_at <  end
  It selects on start_at ONLY. An appointment that begins before the window and
  ends inside it is not returned. The in-memory implementation has the identical
  semantic (backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py:161). Using
  it for collision detection silently misses every long appointment that spans
  the proposed start - the exact case a therapist hits with a 90-minute intake.

CORRECT OVERLAP PREDICATE (half-open intervals, so back-to-back appointments do
NOT collide):
      existing.start_at <  proposed_end
  AND existing.end_at   >  proposed_start

ADD TO THE ABC - backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py:17,
alongside list_by_range (:25):

    @abstractmethod
    def list_overlapping(
        self,
        user_id: str,
        start: str | datetime,
        end: str | datetime,
        *,
        exclude_appointment_id: str | None = None,
    ) -> list[Appointment]:
        ...

  - user_id is the calendar-ownership slice, matching list_by_range and the
    availability engine (see the authorization note at
    backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py:39-52). Do NOT route this
    through the patient_clinicians authorization path - collision detection is
    about one clinician's calendar.
  - exclude_appointment_id exists so a reschedule can ask "would this collide
    with anything OTHER than the appointment I am moving?". Without it, moving
    an appointment by five minutes collides with itself.
  - Cancelled appointments MUST be excluded, in the query, not by the caller.
    Match the existing convention exactly: the codebase compares the bare string
    "cancelled" (backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:80, 212,
    242, 267). Be consistent with that rather than introducing a second spelling.

IMPLEMENT IN BOTH:
  - backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py - mirror list_by_range
    (:71) for session handling, row->model mapping and datetime coercion. Only
    the WHERE clause differs.
  - backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py - the in-memory
    implementation used by every unit test (:161 is the list_by_range twin).
  The two must agree; a divergence here is invisible until production.

OUT OF SCOPE, ON PURPOSE: wiring this into create/update, availability rules,
buffers, and any HTTP surface. This bead ends at "the repository can answer the
question".
acceptance_criteria:
1. list_overlapping is on the AppointmentRepository ABC and implemented in BOTH
   the Postgres and in-memory repositories with identical semantics.
2. Unit tests covering, against BOTH implementations (parametrize or mirror):
   a. Exact same start and end -> collides.
   b. Existing appointment fully contains the proposed slot -> collides.
   c. Proposed slot fully contains an existing appointment -> collides.
   d. Existing starts BEFORE the window and ends inside it -> collides. This is
      the case list_by_range misses; a test that passes with list_by_range's
      predicate has not proven anything.
   e. Back-to-back (existing ends exactly when proposed starts) -> does NOT
      collide.
   f. A cancelled appointment overlapping the slot -> does NOT collide.
   g. exclude_appointment_id omits that appointment from the result.
   h. An appointment belonging to a different user_id -> not returned.
3. `make check` passes at the repo root (lint includes mypy; ruff + pytest alone
   is not sufficient).

title: Split the exploratory pass into generate / execute / classify, driven by personas with motive
description:
Today the exploratory half is one undifferentiated instruction: read the bundle, probe things, write the report. That shape produces a checklist, because generating an idea and testing it compete for the same attention and testing always wins — the model reaches for what it already knows how to run.

Split it into three passes.

GENERATE — no tools. Given the domain-model context pack (PABLO-usn), the hypothesis ledger (PABLO-o42), and a small set of personas, produce a ranked list of hypotheses. Each must be anchored: expressible as a concrete sequence of requests, queries or cloud API calls against the deployed system. Unanchorable ideas are dropped, which is what removes generic filler.

EXECUTE — tools, bounded. Take the top N and attempt them.

CLASSIFY — each attempt resolves to CONFIRMED, REFUTED or PARTIAL, with the observed evidence, and every outcome is written to the ledger.

Personas beat actor labels because a persona forces a completed narrative — an incentive and a constraint — rather than a classification. 'Authenticated user, cross-boundary' is a category; 'an administrator whose access was revoked an hour ago and who wants one more export' is a story that names its own chain steps, and it lands directly on the token-revocation-lag gap the coverage doc already records. Start with three: a curious practitioner poking at a colleague's records inside their own practice, a recently-offboarded administrator, and a party fishing for records they have no lawful claim to.
design: Three separate model invocations, not three sections of one prompt — the separation is the mechanism. GENERATE runs without tool access so it cannot shortcut into executing the first idea. Bound EXECUTE by count and wall clock, and log every tool invocation. CLASSIFY writes to the ledger regardless of outcome, including UNTESTED for hypotheses that ran out of budget, so the next run knows what was left rather than silently re-proposing it. Personas belong in configuration, not hard-coded, so the set can grow without a code change. Out of scope: the deployment target and rules of engagement (tracked separately), and any change to the deterministic checks.
acceptance_criteria:
- Generation, execution and classification are three separate invocations; generation has no tool access.
- Every hypothesis is anchored to a concrete request/query sequence, and unanchorable ones are dropped with a recorded reason.
- Every hypothesis resolves to CONFIRMED / REFUTED / PARTIAL / UNTESTED and is written to the ledger.
- Personas are configuration, not code, and at least three ship with distinct motives.
- Execution is bounded by both count and wall clock, and exceeding either is recorded rather than silent.
- Unit tests cover: unanchored hypothesis dropped, budget exhausted marks UNTESTED, classification written to ledger.
- make check passes.

title: Build a domain-model context pack for the assessment prompt instead of generic security framing
description:
The exploratory half of the assessment is fed category framing, which crowds out the thing that actually produces non-obvious hypotheses: this system's own authorization model.

Concrete example of what is being missed. This application has TWO authorization boundaries — schema-level isolation between practices, and the per-patient clinician grant path (patient_clinicians / has_patient_access, enforced across medications, patient documents and the patient repositories). A model told only 'check for broken access control' will test the first and never consider the second. A model handed both boundaries as facts can ask whether the grant path itself is forgeable through mass assignment on an update endpoint — a specific, testable, non-obvious question that generic framing will never reach.

Assemble the facts the system already collects into a structured context pack and give the exploration prompt that instead: the route table with its auth dependencies annotated, the RLS policy and schema inventory already gathered by the Cloud SQL collector, the grant-table enforcement points, and the egress/subprocessor manifest.
design: Build the pack from existing collector output wherever possible rather than new collection — the Cloud SQL collector already gathers policies and the schema list, and the route table is derivable from the app's own router registration. Keep it structured (not prose) so it is diffable between runs and cheap in context. Pair it with the anchoring constraint the design doc already specifies: a hypothesis that cannot be expressed as concrete requests against the deployed system is omitted. Replace generic category lists rather than adding to them — context budget spent on a checklist is context not spent on the domain. Out of scope: new collectors, changing the deterministic checks.
acceptance_criteria:
- A structured context pack is assembled from existing collector output and passed to the exploration prompt.
- Generic security-category framing is removed from that prompt, not merely supplemented.
- The pack includes both authorization boundaries — schema isolation and the per-patient grant path — as explicit facts.
- A test asserts the pack contains the grant-path facts and that the prompt no longer carries the category list.
- make check passes.

title: Remember refuted hypotheses across runs so a recurring assessment stops re-treading the same ground
description:
A recurring assessment currently diffs FINDINGS between runs but keeps no record of what was hypothesised and then dismissed. Every run therefore starts from zero and re-proposes the same handful of obvious ideas, which is most of why an exploratory pass reads like a generic checklist.

Add a durable hypothesis ledger. Each run appends one record per hypothesis considered: the persona it came from, the objective, the chain sketch expressed as concrete requests or queries, the outcome (CONFIRMED / REFUTED / PARTIAL / UNTESTED), the run id, and the date. Subsequent runs are given the last N runs of the ledger and are instructed that re-proposing a REFUTED chain requires naming what is different this time — a code change, a new route, a changed policy.

This is the forcing function. A model cannot be instructed into novelty, but it can be made unable to repeat itself, and the new ground falls out of the constraint.
design: Store alongside the evidence bundle and persist to the same reports bucket so the ledger survives between runs; read the last N (start with 8) at prompt-build time. Record the chain sketch in the same anchored form the design doc already requires — expressible as a sequence of HTTP requests, SQL queries or cloud API calls against the deployed system — so an entry is checkable rather than a vibe. Out of scope: acting on ledger entries automatically, and any change to how findings are reported.
acceptance_criteria:
- Each run appends one ledger record per hypothesis considered, with outcome.
- The prompt receives the last N runs of ledger entries.
- A run that re-proposes a previously REFUTED chain must state what changed; a test asserts the instruction is present and that the ledger is fed forward.
- The ledger persists between runs and is readable independently of any single report.
- Unit tests cover: append, read-last-N, empty-ledger first run.
- make check passes.

title: The report-writer CLI can silently route around the managed endpoint; the only thing stopping it is a disabled API
description:
Observed 2026-08-02 while reproducing the narrative failure. Running the report-writer CLI locally with GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=true still routed the request through the Code Assist path (cloudaicompanion.googleapis.com) rather than the managed Vertex endpoint, because a user OAuth session was present and the CLI's auth selection preferred it. The env var did not win.

In the production container there is no OAuth session and cloudaicompanion.googleapis.com is not enabled on the target project, so production runs necessarily used the managed endpoint — verified, and the agreement coverage holds today. But that guarantee currently rests on an API happening to be disabled and on an ambient condition in the container, not on anything the runner asserts. A CLI upgrade, a mounted credential, or someone enabling that API for an unrelated reason would silently move the traffic to a different product with different coverage, and nothing in the report would say so.
design: Make the routing explicit rather than incidental. Options in preference order: (1) assert it — before invoking, resolve which endpoint the CLI will use and fail closed if it is not the managed one; (2) record it — write the resolved endpoint and auth mode into the report's attestation block so every archived report states where the text came from; (3) remove the ambiguity — call the managed endpoint directly for the narrative step instead of shelling out to a CLI whose auth precedence is not ours to control. (3) composes well with splitting deterministic synthesis from agentic exploration. Touch points: _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude / _run_cli (~541-590), the attestation block in _assemble_report.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every generated report states, in the attestation block, which endpoint and auth mode produced the narrative.
- A run that cannot confirm the managed endpoint fails rather than proceeding.
- A unit test covers the fail-closed path.
- make check passes.

title: The narrative retry must vary a real parameter, not just append a scold to the same prompt
description: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py::_invoke_llm retries a failed narrative by re-sending the identical prompt with a reinforcement paragraph appended. When the failure mode is a stochastic safety-classifier refusal — confirmed as the cause of the 2026-08-02 run, see PABLO-c2u — that is the same draw twice, and both attempts landed on refuse. A retry that changes nothing material is not a retry. Vary temperature, then model, then provider, in that order, before declaring the narrative dead.
design: Touch points: _invoke_llm (~410), the retry wrapper (~466-500), _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude (~541-572). The gemini CLI takes generation settings via its own flags/config — check what 0.38.x exposes before assuming temperature is reachable; if it is not, escalate straight to the model/provider ladder. Keep _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS as the failure heuristic. Order: attempt 1 default -> attempt 2 reinforced + varied sampling -> attempt 3 alternate model -> fail. Composes with PABLO-c2u (nonzero exit + alternate chaining); land that first if they are worked separately.
acceptance_criteria:
- The second attempt differs from the first by more than appended text — at minimum a changed sampling parameter, and the change is asserted in a unit test.
- A third attempt against the alternate model runs before the run is declared failed.
- Each attempt's model/settings are recorded in the report's attestation block, so a reader can tell which draw produced the narrative.
- Unit tests cover: attempt-1 succeeds (no retry), attempt-2 succeeds, all-fail.
- make check passes.

title: A run whose narrative generation fails must exit nonzero, and must try the alternate model first
description:
The report writer model refused twice on 2026-08-02 and the run still exited 0,
so the scheduled execution reported success while producing an assessment with
no findings and no severity totals. A run that produced nothing analyzable must
not look like a clean run — that is the failure mode that lets a gap sit
unnoticed for a week.

`_invoke_llm` already supports an alternate CLI (`_invoke_claude` exists beside
`_invoke_gemini`), but the two are alternatives chosen up front, not a chain:
when the primary fails its format-failure heuristic twice, nothing tries the
alternate. Two changes: chain the alternate after the primary's second failure,
and exit nonzero when every attempt fails.

Constraint on the alternate: it must be reachable through the same in-agreement
managed endpoint the primary uses (the project's Vertex endpoint), not a public
vendor API. If the alternate is not currently entitled in the target project,
the chaining code still lands and the invocation degrades to the existing
single-model path — the nonzero exit is what must not be deferred.
design: Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py — _invoke_llm (~line 410), the retry wrapper at ~466-500, the NARRATIVE GENERATION FAILED block at ~520, and run()/sys.exit at ~777. _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS (3000) stays the heuristic. Keep the existing narrative-failed report block verbatim; this bead changes control flow and exit status only. Out of scope: changing the prompt text (tracked on the collector bead), changing the format-failure threshold, provisioning the alternate model's entitlement.
acceptance_criteria:
- When the primary model fails the format-failure heuristic on both the initial
  and reinforced attempts, the runner invokes the alternate CLI once before
  giving up.
- When every attempt fails, `run()` returns a nonzero status so the Cloud Run
  Job execution and the dispatching workflow both report failure.
- The report still contains the existing "NARRATIVE GENERATION FAILED" block and
  the intact evidence bundle — failing the run must not suppress the artifact.
- The alternate is invoked against the project's managed Vertex endpoint; no
  public vendor API endpoint or API key is introduced.
- Unit tests: primary-fails-alternate-succeeds (exit 0), all-fail (nonzero exit,
  report still written), primary-succeeds (alternate never invoked).
- `make check` passes.

Cover & scope', and (b) through the real gemini CLI on Vertex with --yolo — also a normal report. title: Move the cross-tenant access probe out of the report-writer prompt and into a deterministic collector
description:
The weekly assessment run on 2026-08-02 produced no narrative: the report writer
model refused the prompt twice (initial + reinforced), quoting back the
active-testing instructions ("executing cross-tenant IDOR attacks against
specific API endpoints", "conducting dynamic exploitation ... against concrete
web applications"). The evidence bundle collected normally; only the narrative
is missing, so the run yielded no findings and no severity totals.

Reproduction is confirmed and the cause is the prompt's shape, not access:
calling the same model, same region, same project directly with a prompt that
retains the "validate cross-tenant IDOR against these endpoints" instruction
gets a refusal; the identical call with that instruction removed — asking only
for a write-up of already-collected scanner output — returns a normal response.
The model identifier has been unchanged across all 14 archived reports, so the
variable is the safety tuning behind a preview alias, which moves without a
version bump. Nothing to request from the vendor; the prompt is ours to fix.

The durable fix is not prompt-wrangling. STEP 4 of `_build_prompt` asks the
model to *perform* the cross-tenant probe — the single most important check in
the whole assessment — which means the result depends on a model being willing
and is not reproducible for audit. Move that probe into a deterministic
collector alongside the other collectors, and let the narrative step report a
result that was already established.
design: Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_collectors.py (new collector, mirror the shape of the existing collectors and their bundle-summary entries), backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py::_build_prompt STEP 4 and STEP 5 (lines ~370-395). The two ephemeral identities are already provisioned by backend/app/jobs/pentest_identity.py and reach the prompt as PENTEST_TEST_ID_TOKEN_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_EMAIL_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_UID_A/B — the collector reads the same values. Severity classification for a FAIL stays where it already lives (backend/app/jobs/pentest_severity.py); the collector reports the observation, not the tier. Out of scope: adding new probe classes (intra-tenant IDOR is tracked separately), changing which scanners run, any IAM or infrastructure change.
acceptance_criteria:
- A new collector (e.g. `collect_cross_tenant_idor` in
  `backend/app/jobs/pentest_collectors.py`) performs the A/B probe with the two
  already-provisioned ephemeral identities: A creates a patient + session via
  the authenticated API, B re-probes those UUIDs, 404 = PASS, 200 = FAIL, and
  records created by A are cleaned up before the collector returns.
- The collector writes a structured PASS/FAIL result plus the probed paths into
  the evidence bundle, and appears in the bundle summary table like every other
  collector (ok / error / skipped, with a note).
- `_build_prompt` STEP 4 no longer instructs the model to execute the probe; it
  instructs the model to report the collector's recorded result. STEP 5's
  "targeted curl against *.run.app" agency clause is likewise narrowed to
  read-only evidence gathering.
- Unit tests cover: collector PASS path, collector FAIL path, collector error
  path, and cleanup-on-exception. A prompt test asserts the string
  "Exercise cross-tenant IDOR" is gone.
- `make check` (lint incl. mypy + test) passes.

title: Note-type registry: per-definition system prompt for generation
description:
## Problem

The note-generation pipeline is registry-driven: a NoteTypeDefinition can supply a custom user-prompt builder (`prompt_builder`), and every other type gets a prompt auto-synthesized from its fields' `ai_hint`s. But the SYSTEM prompt is fixed: `_DEFAULT_GENERATION_PROMPT_SYSTEM` (backend/app/services/note_generation_service.py:95) frames every transcript as a therapy session and instructs "clinically-appropriate language", with SOAP the only exception (SOAP_SYSTEM_PROMPT).

A registered note type whose format is not classic clinical narration (e.g. a supervision case review, a practice/admin format, or any downstream-registered format) can only fight the clinical system framing from inside the user prompt. That works but is fragile — the two prompts pull in different directions.

## Design

1. `NoteTypeDefinition` (backend/app/notes/registry.py) gains an optional `system_prompt: str | None = None` (a plain string, not a builder — system prompts are static per format; use `field(compare=False)` only if needed to keep dataclass equality semantics unchanged for existing tests).
2. `RegistryNoteGenerationService._generate_via_registry` (backend/app/services/note_generation_service.py:214-232) selects the system prompt in this order:
   - `definition.system_prompt` when set;
   - else `SOAP_SYSTEM_PROMPT` when `definition.key == SOAP_KEY` (unchanged);
   - else `_DEFAULT_GENERATION_PROMPT_SYSTEM` (unchanged).
   The selection must apply on BOTH branches (custom `prompt_builder` and auto-synthesized user prompt).
3. NOT exposed over the API: `NoteTypeSchema` in backend/app/routes/note_types.py must not serialize `system_prompt` (prompt text is server-side config, same as `prompt_builder` today).
4. No behavior change for any currently-registered type: `soap` and `narrative` definitions do not set the field.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `NoteTypeDefinition(system_prompt="...")` compiles and registers; default is None.
- [ ] Generation for a definition WITH `system_prompt` sends exactly that string as the system prompt (assert via the fake/mock LLM gateway capture in backend/tests/test_note_generation_service.py).
- [ ] Generation for `soap` still sends SOAP_SYSTEM_PROMPT; a hint-synthesized type without the field still sends the default (regression assertions).
- [ ] The custom-`prompt_builder` branch also honors `system_prompt` (test with a definition that sets both).
- [ ] `GET /api/note-types` response shape is unchanged (no `system_prompt` key) — assert in backend/tests/test_note_types_api.py.
- [ ] `make check` green (ruff + mypy + full pytest).

## Files

- backend/app/notes/registry.py (field)
- backend/app/services/note_generation_service.py (selection)
- backend/tests/test_notes_registry.py, backend/tests/test_note_generation_service.py, backend/tests/test_note_types_api.py

Small, self-contained, no DB/schema/API-surface change.

title: Backend integration tests for chat — real Postgres via testcontainers
description:
Chat's backend coverage is unit-grade only: test_chat_turn_service.py uses InMemoryChatRepository (no DB constraints), test_chat_llm_gateway.py uses FakeChatLLMGateway, test_chat_prompts.py is module-level. DB-only failure modes have escaped to deployments twice: the ck_chat_messages_content_len CHECK-constraint 500 (in-memory repos don't enforce CHECKs), and a has_patient_access SQL bind-param bug. Both would have been caught by integration tests against a real database.

NEEDED: backend/tests/integration/test_chat_real_db.py running against testcontainers Postgres (already in dev deps; see existing backend/tests/integration/ suite for the container fixture pattern). Cases:
1. Create conversation + empty placeholder message + finalize — exercises the content_len CHECK + forensic-row pattern.
2. Empty patient + 'what can you tell me' — prompt resolution + empty-chart marker land on the stored conversation with an empty context manifest.
3. Multi-turn (3 turns) — conversation_messages.sequence increments, manifest recorded per turn.

title: Dependabot auto-merge runs no post-merge workflows: merge with an App token
description:
'.github/workflows/dependabot-automerge.yml' merges with 'GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}'. GitHub deliberately does not trigger push-based workflows for commits pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN, so nothing runs on the resulting merge commit: no CI, no Release, no Deploy.

Consequences on main:
  - No container image is published for those commits, so anything that pins a specific main SHA cannot resolve an image for it.
  - There is no post-merge verification at all on the default branch, so a merge that is green as a PR is never re-checked against main.
  - The gap is silent. Nothing reports failure; the workflows simply never start.

Observed on main 2026-07-25/26: commits from #613 and #617 have zero workflow runs (only CodeQL, which triggers on a different event). #619, merged by a person the same day, ran CI, Release and Deploy normally. That contrast is the whole bug.

Note this is unrelated to #612, which changed WHICH pull requests qualify for auto-merge (gating on pull_request.user.login rather than the spoofable github.actor). That fix is correct and still needed; it just does not affect which token performs the merge.

Fix: mint a short-lived GitHub App token (actions/create-github-app-token) and merge with that instead, so the merge is attributed to the App and downstream push workflows fire. Verify by confirming a Release run and a published image exist for the next auto-merged commit.
notes:
NOT SUITABLE FOR UNATTENDED AUTOMATION — needs a maintainer, assessed 2026-07-26.

Two reasons, both structural rather than a matter of difficulty:

1. Not self-contained. The fix is only partly a repo change. It also requires a GitHub App installed on this repository and its APP_ID / APP_PRIVATE_KEY provisioned as repo secrets — console and credential work that cannot be done from a checkout, and that no automated run should be doing.

2. No done-signal any pre-merge check can adjudicate. Correctness here means 'a later auto-merged dependency PR produces a Release run and a published image'. CI can validate workflow syntax; it cannot observe post-merge trigger behaviour. That is exactly why this went unnoticed across two merges on 2026-07-25/26.

It is also small: once the App and secrets exist, the workflow edit is a few lines, and the pattern is already written and commented in a sibling repository's base-bump workflow. Verification is observational — watch the next auto-merged dependency PR and confirm a Release run and image exist for its commit.

title: Pin fastapi <0.140: 0.140 retains dependency callables and leaks DB engines
description:
fastapi 0.140.0 adds three process-global caches in fastapi/dependencies/models.py:

  @lru_cache(maxsize=1024)
  def _is_gen_callable_cached(call_identity: _CallIdentity) -> bool

keyed by _CallIdentity, which holds a STRONG reference to the dependency callable (self.call is other.call). 0.139 has no such caches.

A session dependency is typically a closure capturing a SQLAlchemy Engine. Pinning the callable pins the closure, which pins the engine and its connection pool. SQLAlchemy releases pooled sockets on engine finalization, so a pinned engine never closes its connections. Any test suite that constructs many app instances therefore accumulates open connections until Postgres max_connections (default 100) is exhausted, failing with 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already'.

Measured, holding every other dependency constant (sqlalchemy, psycopg2, testcontainers identical; only fastapi varied):
  - engines still reachable after gc.collect(): 50/50 under 0.140.0, 1/50 under 0.139.0
  - an integration suite that builds many apps: 93 failed / 219 passed under 0.140.0, clean under 0.139.0

Not a per-request regression: dependency cache sharing is unchanged (1 session opened and closed per request in both versions), so a single long-lived app process is not affected -- the engine there is already cached for the process lifetime.

Fix: constrain fastapi to >=0.139.0,<0.140 in pyproject.toml and relock. No security exposure in staying on 0.139.0 -- the only fastapi advisories are GHSA-8h2j-cgx8-6xv7 (< 0.65.2) and GHSA-qf9m-vfgh-m389 (<= 0.109.0).

Follow-up: report upstream (a global lru_cache strong-keyed on user callables retains everything those callables close over), then lift the pin once released.
notes: Verified on main: pyproject.toml pins fastapi = ">=0.139.0,<0.140", landed in #619 ("Pin fastapi below 0.140 to stop engines leaking in test runs"). 0.140's module-level dependency-callable caches can no longer be installed, so the engine-retention leak this issue tracks is closed off at the dependency boundary.
close_reason: Pin landed in #619 — main has fastapi >=0.139.0,<0.140.

title: Session validity: read-only session peek endpoint + server-driven idle controller
description: The client-side idle timer and the server idle clock (Redis) run independently, so a restored tab can render the app while the backend session is already expired, and the warning dialog can promise 'stay signed in' without extending the server session. Plan: (1) GET /api/auth/session — read-only peek returning {enforced, active, seconds_remaining} that does NOT refresh the activity TTL; (2) POST /api/auth/session/touch — explicit keep-alive; (3) rework IdleTimeout to validate the session on mount/pageshow/visibilitychange and poll, driving the countdown from the server clock, with the current local-clock behavior kept as fallback when enforcement is off (no Redis); (4) route SSE and blob-download 401s through the same forced-logout path as apiClient; (5) carry a reason param on the dashboard layout's dead-session redirect and let /login render for forced-logout arrivals instead of bouncing valid-cookie users back to /dashboard.
notes: PR #557 open (feat/session-validity-controller). Backend peek/touch endpoints + server-driven IdleTimeout controller + SSE/blob forced-logout unification + login-bounce fix. All suites green (2093 backend, 961 frontend, ruff+mypy clean).

title: Terminal token-expiry 401 strands the user instead of redirecting to /login
description:
When a client-managed session terminally expires (the id token is expired AND the force-refresh retry cannot mint a valid token — e.g. the refresh token itself has expired after long inactivity, the account was disabled, or getIdToken returns null), an API call such as opening a patient comes back 401 and the user is NOT redirected to the login screen. They stay on a logged-in-looking page that renders a generic error.

Root cause: frontend/src/lib/api/client.ts only redirects to /login for the IDLE_TIMEOUT error code (handleIdleTimeoutLogout, ~line 239-245). The recoverable token path (TOKEN_EXPIRED/INVALID_TOKEN) force-refreshes and retries once (PR #300, ~line 189-194), but if that retry is STILL 401 it falls through to 'throw apiError' with no redirect. Next.js middleware doesn't catch it because the request is a client-side XHR, not a full navigation.

Fix: after the force-refresh retry, if a token-level 401 (TOKEN_EXPIRED/INVALID_TOKEN) persists — or the auth header could not be minted — treat it as terminal: signOut() + redirect to /login?reason=session_expired, mirroring handleIdleTimeoutLogout including its re-entry guard (a dashboard load fires several parallel requests, so a burst of 401s must produce ONE redirect, not many).
acceptance_criteria: A terminally-expired session that 401s on a client-side API call (post-refresh-retry, non-IDLE_TIMEOUT token code, or missing-token) signs the user out and redirects to /login?reason=session_expired; a parallel burst of such 401s fires exactly one redirect.
notes: Fix + tests in pablo PR #536 (fix/terminal-token-401-redirect)

title: SOAP generation worker holds a DB connection across the model call
description:
generate_session_note (the async SOAP worker) loads the session, patient, and existing-note rows, which opens a read transaction and checks out a pooled connection. Nothing commits it before _generate_and_persist_note runs the multi-second model call, so the connection sits idle-in-transaction for the whole generation. On longer transcripts the server/proxy drops the idle connection; the note INSERT afterward then fails with OperationalError ('SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly') followed by PendingRollbackError, the note never persists, and the Cloud Tasks job retries the same session indefinitely (500 each time). The method's own comment already claims 'the LLM call runs with no open DB transaction' -- but no commit exists between the SELECTs and the model call.

Fix: commit the read transaction (release the pooled connection) immediately before generation, matching the either-side-of-the-LLM pattern upload_session already uses. expire_on_commit=False keeps the loaded session/patient usable, transcript is a JSONB column (no lazy reload), and the note INSERT autobegins a fresh pre-pinged connection that the checkout/after_begin listeners re-arm with search_path + RLS. Short transcripts hid the bug (generation finishes before the idle connection is dropped).

title: Stale Firebase session wedges the auth boot on sign-in
description:
useFirebaseAuthState awaited getIdToken() and the /api/login cookie sync before clearing its loading state, with no error handling. When a browser profile holds a restored Firebase session whose refresh token has expired, getIdToken() rejects, the onIdTokenChanged listener dies before setLoading(false), and the app is stuck on the loading splash (loading stays true, user stays null, so the redirect to /dashboard never fires). The existing stuck-state recovery only matches one specific SDK assertion, not a rejected refresh. Sign-in succeeds at the backend but the SPA never advances; a clean profile works because there is no stale token to refresh.

Fix (PR #502): wrap the listener in try/finally so loading always clears, bound the token refresh and cookie sync with a timeout, and on failure drop the stale session (signOut + wipe the persisted auth record + clear the cookie) so the next attempt starts clean. Cookie sync stays awaited on the success path because route middleware gates /dashboard on it. Adds client.test.ts.
notes: Follow-up fix in PR #504 (fix/auth-boot-transient-fetch): split getIdToken-reject (clear session) from cookie-sync failure (non-fatal, keep session, warn-level). Extracted syncAuthTick + 4 regression tests. Awaiting CI -> ship -> dev smoke must pass -> prod.
close_reason: Recover from a stale Firebase session instead of hanging the auth boot — OSS PR #502

title: Passkey-first onboarding leaves the new session without a second-factor claim (403 on PHI routes)
description:
Symptom: after completing onboarding with a passkey as the second factor, the user lands on the dashboard but every PHI route (e.g. GET /api/patients, GET /api/sessions) returns 403 MFA_REQUIRED. Confirmed in a live deployment; signing out and signing back in *with the passkey* clears it.

Root cause: require_mfa accepts a session only if the ID token carries firebase.sign_in_second_factor (Firebase TOTP/SMS) OR pablo_amr: ["webauthn"] (see backend/app/auth/providers.py:second_factor_satisfied). The pablo_amr claim is minted ONLY by POST /api/auth/passkey/authenticate/finish. Onboarding runs register/begin + register/finish (backend/app/routes/passkey.py): register/finish sets mfa_enrolled_at (which completes onboarding) and issues backup codes, but never mints a second-factor token. So the just-enrolled session holds a first-factor-only token and is blocked from all PHI until the user signs out and signs back in via the passkey (which runs the authenticate ceremony). Enrolling a passkey != the session has cleared MFA, and nothing in the onboarding flow does the step-up.

Impact: blocks 100% of passkey-first onboards from accessing any patient data on their first session. Launch-relevant.

Preferred fix: have POST /api/auth/passkey/register/finish mint and return a pablo_amr custom token on a successful attestation. A verified attestation proves possession of the authenticator at that moment, just like an assertion, so it is legitimate to treat the freshly-enrolled session as second-factor-satisfied. The client then signs in with the returned custom token and force-refreshes the Firebase ID token before redirecting to the dashboard — no second WebAuthn ceremony, no sign-out/in. One ceremony total.

Rejected alternative: client runs the authenticate ceremony immediately after register/finish. Makes the user effectively perform the WebAuthn ceremony twice.

Acceptance:
- A brand-new passkey-first onboard can load patient data immediately after finishing onboarding, with no sign-out/in.
- register/finish returns a token (or signal) the client uses to obtain an ID token whose claims satisfy second_factor_satisfied.
- Regression test: a session established directly from register/finish (first enrollment) passes require_mfa. Keep the existing authenticate/finish -> pablo_amr path working.
- Note for the second-passkey-from-settings case: that session is already MFA-satisfied, so minting is redundant but harmless; ensure it does not regress.
notes: PR pablo#494 (backend mint + OSS api type). Paired SaaS overlay consumer: pablo-saas#707 / THERAPY-rokd (RED until base-bump).

title: Fresh sign-in 500s: legacy subject-id fallback feeds a non-uuid into users.id lookup
description: _resolve_pablo_user_id(create_if_missing=False) falls back to the provider subject id when no user_identities mapping exists ('user provisioned before the indirection table'). Post-remap, users.id is uuid and no row carries a provider uid, so the fallback can only produce a value that EXPLODES the subsequent user_repo.get() with psycopg2 InvalidTextRepresentation — turning 'no user yet' (which should proceed to the allowlist+create path) into a 500 on /users/me/status, PATCH /users/me, ext/auth/check-status for every brand-new user. Fix: PostgresUserRepository.get() returns None for non-uuid ids (the semantically-correct 'no such user'); the legacy fallback then degrades gracefully everywhere.

title: Tenant provisioning 500s: heal-RLS migration's module-level app.db import breaks alembic stamp
description: b6e1d8c4a7f2_heal_tenant_rls_policies.py (PR #450) imports app.db.enable_rls_on_schema at module level. create_practice_schema's _stamp_alembic_at_head walks the revision graph, which imports every migration module — in runtime contexts where the app package isn't on sys.path the stamp raises ModuleNotFoundError and tenant provisioning 500s. Defer the import into upgrade(); migration modules must stay importable without the application package.

title: apiClient chokes on 204/empty-body JSON responses — mutations silently fail after success
description: apiClient's success path calls response.json() whenever content-type includes application/json, but FastAPI 204 responses carry content-type: application/json with an EMPTY body — .json() throws 'Unexpected end of JSON input', the mutation lands in onError, and onSuccess cache invalidation never runs. Symptom: compliance DocumentsDialog 'Remove' deletes server-side (204) but the row never leaves the list. Any del() against a 204 route hits this class. Fix: short-circuit 204 (and empty bodies) to undefined before parsing.

title: Pentest tenant provisioning 500s: owner_user_id empty-string sentinel vs uuid column
description: pentest_tenant_service.provision() still writes owner_user_id='' when creating the PracticeRow, but practices.owner_user_id is uuid (nullable) since the Phase-C cast — Postgres rejects ''::uuid with InvalidTextRepresentation, so every pentest/e2e tenant provision 500s. Write None instead ('' was the legacy not-set sentinel; the cast maps ''->NULL and dropped NOT NULL for exactly this).

Add a documents affordance to each compliance item row (paperclip + count) that opens a dialog to: list attached documents, upload a new one (file picker + document_type), download, and delete. Wire the existing endpoints through a typed API client + react-query hooks. This turns the compliance panel into a credential vault: track the obligation AND hold the proof.

title: Add validated misuse-risk screeners (ORT, SOAPP, DIRE) as scored instruments
description: Add the Opioid Risk Tool (ORT), SOAPP, and DIRE as scored screening instruments in the existing instrument/outcome-measure framework, alongside PHQ-9 / GAD-7 (items -> score -> risk band). Step 1: licensing/free-use determination per instrument (same diligence as the PHQ-9/GAD-7 analysis) — bundle only those cleared for free reproduction. Original/cleared wording only, cited. Quick win: reuses the scored-instrument plumbing; no engine changes. Primary refs: Webster 2005 (ORT); Belgrade 2006 (DIRE); SOAPP/SOAPP-R (check current terms).
design: Framework (OSS main): instruments are pure data in backend/app/outcome_measures/instruments.py INSTRUMENT_REGISTRY (InstrumentDefinition + SeverityBand); add frontend InstrumentMeta in frontend/src/lib/outcomeMeasures.ts; per-tenant outcome_measures table is generic (NO migration). Findings: (1) DIRE (7 items x1-3, summed) and SOAPP-R (24 x0-4, summed) fit the uniform item_min/item_max + simple compute_total model. (2) ORT does NOT — items have different weighted point values and several are SEX-CONDITIONAL (e.g. family hx alcohol abuse scores differently M vs F); needs a per-item / sex-aware scoring extension to compute_total (currently a plain sum; code comments already note per-item weighting is 'reserved for future'). (3) Licensing: ORT (Webster 2005) + DIRE (Belgrade 2006) freely reproduced -> bundle candidates; SOAPP-R is (c) Inflexxion (registration historically required) -> likely cite-only, HOLD from OSS bundling pending legal. Recommended scope: extend scoring for weighted/conditional instruments, ship DIRE + ORT as draft (free-use determination flagged like the PHQ-9 analysis), hold SOAPP. Mark instruments draft until the same clinical+legal sign-off as PHQ-9/GAD-7 content.
notes: DIRE landed at the engine/API layer (PR #383, branch feat/risk-screeners): data-only add, 71 tests + mypy + ruff green. Remaining under this umbrella: (1) frontend per-item response anchors + DIRE entry form (DIRE's anchors differ per item; current InstrumentMeta has one shared scale); (2) ORT — needs weighted + sex-conditional scoring (does not fit the uniform per-item model); (3) SOAPP-R held on copyright (Inflexxion). See follow-up beads.

title: Clinician must author/review bundled MDD/GAD criterion wording before any clinical use
description:
GATE before the diagnostic engine's bundled content is exposed in any real/clinical deployment.

The MDD/GAD criterion + gate wording in backend/app/diagnostics/baseline.py (BASELINE_DEFINITIONS) is original DRAFT content, almost certainly AI-drafted (PR #378), committed without AI attribution and NOT authored or reviewed by a clinician. The structure tracks DSM-5 closely (5-of-9 + 2 cardinals + exclusion gates; GAD worry + 3-of-6 + 6mo).

Two risks:
1. Clinical accuracy — an LLM paraphrase can be subtly wrong in a tool that SUGGESTS a diagnosis (patient-safety surface). Determination is clinician-confirmed, but the criterion text is presented as authoritative.
2. Copyright — a paraphrase of DSM-5 criteria can still be a derivative of APA-copyrighted text even with no verbatim copying. 'We paraphrased it' is not automatically a clean-room defense.

Done so far: record dialog now shows a 'Draft criteria — for clinical review before clinical use; not a substitute for clinical judgment' notice (PABLO-6xj.2, PR #381, commit 4c4f33b). Draft doc for review: docs/architecture/diagnostic-content-mdd.draft.md (uncommitted).

Required: (a) the clinical lead authors or rewrites _MDD/_GAD wording and signs off; (b) explicit decision on the DSM-5 derivative/copyright question (legal sanity check); (c) only then remove/relax the draft marker. Until both, treat bundled content as draft-only.
notes: Author MDD/GAD as clinician-authored CHECKLISTS (clinician marks which symptoms apply; no X-of-Y threshold, no auto 'meets criteria') sourced solely from PHQ-9/GAD-7 (Pfizer free-use grant) + peer-reviewed open literature; ICD-11 cite-only. Sourcing analysis (AI-drafted, pending human clinical + legal review): pablo-saas docs/compliance/diagnostic-symptom-sourcing-research.md. Gates before bundling any content / relaxing the in-product draft marker: (1) clinical-lead authorship + sign-off; (2) legal sign-off on the PHQ-9/GAD-7 grant + non-DSM provenance. Engine + public-domain ICD-10-CM catalog already in place; no definitions bundled by default.

title: enable_rls_on_schema leaves three tenant tables deny-all (FORCE RLS, no policy)
description:
enable_rls_on_schema (backend/app/db/__init__.py) selects every tenant table that has a user_id, patient_id, or id column, then ENABLE+FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY at the top of the loop *before* deciding a policy. It then creates a policy only for known shapes (patient_documents, patient_clinicians, patients, any-user_id, any-patient_id, chat_messages). A table that has only an 'id' column and matches no shape ends up force-RLS'd with NO policy = deny-all: under a NOBYPASSRLS role every read returns 0 rows and every write affects 0 rows, silently.

Audit of the current tenant template finds THREE such tables:
  - compliance_documents — owns rows via uploaded_by_user_id (NOT NULL); the code only checks the literal column name user_id, so it misses this owner column. LIVE feature (compliance_document repo get/list/query).
  - ehr_routes — no ownership column at all (ehr_system/route_name/steps); tenant-level config like ehr_prompts, which is correctly skipped only because it lacks an id column. LIVE feature (ehr_route repo).
  - users — vestigial per-tenant table, unused at runtime (identity lives in the platform schema); a Firestore-migration relic, frozen at an older column shape.

Only invisible until the role lost BYPASSRLS — BYPASSRLS ignores RLS entirely, so deny-all read fine. Existing tenants were not backfilled, so the blast radius is tenants provisioned after the role flip: their compliance-document and EHR-route features silently return nothing.

The chat_messages branch already documents this exact trap ('the loop ENABLE+FORCEs RLS but leaves no policy, which is a deny-all configuration that only the BYPASSRLS-on-role posture mistakenly hides in production') — these three tables are the siblings nobody added branches for.

FIX:
  1. compliance_documents — add a policy keyed on uploaded_by_user_id (USING + WITH CHECK). uploaded_by_user_id is NOT NULL; prefer it over the nullable compliance_item_id parent so orphan documents are not hidden.
  2. ehr_routes + users — treat as not-row-scoped (search_path is their boundary): do NOT force RLS on them (idempotently DISABLE to heal any tenant already provisioned wrong). users is also slated for removal (see cleanup below).
  3. Fail-loud guard: restructure so RLS is only forced when a policy is attached (or the table is on an explicit not-row-scoped list); raise on any id/user_id/patient_id table that matches neither, so a future table cannot silently become deny-all.
  4. Regression test: provision a schema, assert every table with relrowsecurity/relforcerowsecurity has >=1 policy (no deny-all), and that the known config tables are intentionally unforced.

CLEANUP (separate, lower priority): the per-tenant users table is a vestigial Firestore-migration artifact (identity lives in the platform schema; the per-tenant copy is frozen at an older shape and read by nothing). It is auto-generated into tenant_template.sql from the tenant alembic chain, so removing it needs a tenant migration + regen_tenant_template.py, not a hand-edit. Drop it once the RLS fix lands.
notes:
Fix in PR #348 (branch fix/tenant-rls-deny-all-tables). compliance_documents -> uploaded_by_user_id policy; ehr_routes + users left not-row-scoped (RLS disabled idempotently); fail-loud else-branch for any future force-RLS-without-policy table; unit test test_enable_rls_policy_coverage.py (5 cases). ruff + format clean, mypy clean for the diff, tests pass. FOLLOW-UP: existing schemas provisioned while these tables were deny-all are only healed when enable_rls_on_schema runs again — run enable_rls_on_all_practice_schemas() after this deploys to re-apply across existing tenants. Vestigial per-tenant users table drop (migration + regen_tenant_template.py) tracked as separate cleanup.
VERIFIED ON PROD 2026-06-01 (pg_class/pg_policies): ALL 9 practice_* tenant schemas have compliance_documents, ehr_routes, and users at relforcerowsecurity=true with 0 policies = deny-all. Correction to earlier note: this is NOT limited to tenants provisioned after the role flip — enable_rls_on_schema runs at provision time, so every tenant got these 3 tables force-RLS'd-without-policy at creation. The NOBYPASSRLS flip (2026-05-31) activated the deny-all across all existing tenants simultaneously. compliance_documents + ehr_routes are live features and are currently returning zero rows on every prod tenant under the pablo role. Heal = run enable_rls_on_all_practice_schemas() once this fix deploys (or apply the corrective SQL directly).
Prod hotfix applied 2026-06-01 across all 8 existing tenant schemas (idempotent loop matching this PR's logic) — verified compliance_documents enabled+policy 8/8, ehr_routes/users RLS-disabled 8/8. Existing tenants healed; this PR makes the tenant-creation path (enable_rls_on_schema via create_practice_schema) correct for new tenants. NB: until this deploys, a new signup runs the old code and would re-introduce the deny-all, so land promptly.
close_reason: Merged to main via PR #348 (squash 0b910e1). enable_rls_on_schema now: compliance_documents gets a uploaded_by_user_id policy; ehr_routes/users left not-row-scoped (RLS disabled, idempotent heal); fails loud on any future force-RLS-without-policy table; unit test added. All 16 CI checks green incl. Backend integration (Postgres). Existing 8 prod tenants already healed by hotfix; new tenants correct by construction. Deploy to dev/prod rides the base-image bump chain (pablo-saas).

(b) The after_begin _rearm_rls_user_id_on_txn_begin listener (re-arms app.current_user_id after mid-request commits) has ZERO test coverage; a regression -> silent zero-rows under RLS in mid-request queries. title: Audit writes: enforce tenant scope + surface failures via a pluggable notifier
description: Audit entries are written to tenant-scoped tables (audit_logs) resolved by the connection search_path. Two integrity gaps: (1) the write relies on AMBIENT search_path — a write on a connection without an established tenant context can resolve against the wrong/no schema, yielding an inaccurate or cross-contaminated audit trail (an authoritative record that under-reports for one tenant and is polluted for another); (2) the audit service currently SWALLOWS write failures (best-effort log), so a dropped entry is silent — undetectable incompleteness. Harden: (a) assert an established tenant context before an audit write (fail loudly if absent) instead of relying on ambient state; (b) replace the silent swallow with a structured, high-severity 'audit integrity' event emitted through a PLUGGABLE AuditFailureNotifier interface (default impl: structured CRITICAL log line with a stable, machine-consumable marker). Self-hosters can register their own notifier (webhook/pager). No audit entry should be lost without a loud, queryable signal. Pre-launch hardening.

title: Reset connection search_path on pool checkin + pooled-connection isolation test
description: search_path is set session-level (SET, not SET LOCAL), so it persists on a pooled connection after a request ends. The Engine 'checkout' listener re-applies it from the request context var, but no-ops when that var is unset (background/worker/standalone checkouts), so such a checkout inherits the previous request's tenant schema. RLS (transaction-local app.current_user_id) normally degrades this to zero rows, but the connection itself is never returned to a neutral state. Add a connection 'checkin' reset (SET search_path = public, or DISCARD ALL on the post-rollback connection) so pooled connections return neutral and a checkout that forgets to set a schema fails closed instead of inheriting the last tenant — a connection-layer guarantee independent of RLS. Plus an integration test exercising the fail-open direction: arm tenant A on a connection, return it to the pool, run a query in a context without A's grant on the same connection, assert zero rows / no A data. Pairs the checkin reset with the test that proves it.
notes: PR pablo#328. Engine checkin listener: SET search_path=public on every connection return (not DISCARD ALL, to preserve timeout GUCs); psycopg2 autocommit-toggled so it doesn't leave an open txn breaking pool_pre_ping. Integration test forces single-connection reuse (pool_size=1 + pg_backend_pid across all 3 checkouts) and proves both directions; verified it fails with the reset disabled. make check green. Review-required.

title: Pentest severity rollup uses substring match on report prose — every run trips HIGH/CRITICAL alert
description:
Background
==========

`pentest_runner._highest_severity()` returns "CRITICAL" if the literal
string "CRITICAL" appears anywhere in the assembled report markdown:

    def _highest_severity(report: str) -> str:
        for token in ("CRITICAL", "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"):
            if token in report:
                return token
        return "NONE"

Every report inevitably contains the word "CRITICAL" — in the
executive summary ("**CRITICAL:** 0 findings"), in the methodology
prose, and most damningly in **Appendix C: Severity Rubric** which
defines what CRITICAL means. So every run logs `severity=CRITICAL`
regardless of the actual finding set.

This was masked for weeks because `_notify_high_finding` was emitting
via the default Python logger (which doesn't end up in
`jsonPayload.severity`), so the Cloud Logging alert policy silently
missed every prior run. Once `_notify_high_finding` was fixed to emit
structured JSON the policy filters on, the underlying false-positive
in `_highest_severity` started paging on every run.

Confirmed across runs 2026-05-18, 2026-05-24, and 2026-05-25 — all
three logged `severity=CRITICAL` despite having zero findings in the
narrative.

Connected bug
=============

`_count_findings_by_severity` is the sibling function the author
clearly intended to be the right pattern (comment: "avoids re-parsing
the LLM narrative for severity counts"). But it counts rows by
matching `| CRITICAL |` against the report — i.e. it expects the LLM
to render findings in a `| Severity | Title | Location | ... |`
table. The current narrative renders findings as bullet prose
("**MEDIUM:** 1 finding") instead, so this function has been
returning `{CRITICAL: 0, HIGH: 0, MEDIUM: 0, LOW: 0}` for every run,
including ones with real medium findings.

Both bugs share a root cause: alerting is computed from the LLM-
generated markdown rather than from the structured scanner outputs
the runner already has in hand.

Fix
===

The collectors already produce structured `by_severity` dicts as part
of each artifact's summary (`run_trivy_image`, `run_pip_audit`, etc.).
Roll severity up deterministically from those, not from the report
prose. Keep the LLM in the narrative role only — it makes the report
readable, but it does not have the pager.

Concretely:

1. Compute `finding_counts` and `highest_severity` from
   `artifact.summary["by_severity"]` aggregated across collectors,
   before the LLM call.
2. Pass those values into the prompt so the narrative is constrained
   to match (LLM cannot drift the severity).
3. Replace both `_highest_severity` and `_count_findings_by_severity`
   to read from the pre-computed counts, not the assembled report.
4. Add a `pentest/suppressions.yaml` for tracked false-positives and
   context-aware downgrades (e.g. semgrep `sqlalchemy.text` flags
   with bound params; `urllib` usage in `pentest_identity.py`).
   Schema: `{tool, finding_id, downgrade_to, reason, expires_on,
   approved_by}`. Apply suppressions during the deterministic rollup,
   not in prose.

Why this matters
================

This is a HIPAA-relevant alert path. The automated pentest mechanism
contributes to §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (continuous risk analysis) and
to the §164.314(a) written-verification trail. An alert that fires on
every run trains the operator to ignore it — alert fatigue is the
failure mode that masks the next real finding. The substring bug
makes the alert literally untrustable.

Concrete evidence
=================

- Latest run report (compliance bucket): pentest/2026-05-25T20-41-02Z-
  a41fa42f.md, narrative summary 0 critical, 0 high, 1 medium, 3 low
- Log line: `Pentest report=... severity=CRITICAL`
- Same log line for runs 2026-05-18, 2026-05-24, 2026-05-25
- Cloud Logging alert policy filters on `jsonPayload.alert_type=
  "pentest_high"` emitted by `_notify_high_finding`

Out of scope
============

- Adding a UI for managing suppressions. `pentest/suppressions.yaml`
  + git review is sufficient.
- Migrating away from the LLM narrative. The judgment value is real;
  it just shouldn't drive alerting.
- Backfilling severity for prior runs in the audit log.

title: Patient list has no pagination — UI caps at 20 rows
description:
## Problem

\`PatientTable.tsx\` calls \`usePatientList({ search })\` with no \`page_size\` and no \`page\` controls. The backend default is \`page_size=20\` (\`backend/app/routes/patients.py:163\`), so the UI silently truncates to the first 20 patients sorted by last_name, first_name. There is no Next/Prev, no \"showing N of M\", and no way for a clinician with 21+ patients to reach the rest of their roster except by typing into the search box.

The backend response already returns \`total\` alongside \`data\` (\`PatientListResponse\`), so the data is there — the UI just discards it.

## Why it matters

For solo therapists this caps usable size at 20 active clients. As soon as one provider has more — totally normal for an established practice — they cannot see their full list without searching by name (which has its own UX issues, see [[patient-search-needs-improvement]]).

## Options

1. **Add pagination controls.** Standard Prev/Next + page indicator. Honest \"showing 1-20 of N\" framing. Minimal change.
2. **Increase the default page_size + infinite scroll.** Friendlier on small lists. More work, but matches how the table feels for someone with 35 patients.
3. **Increase the default page_size to 100 and call it a day.** API max is already 100; cheapest fix. Caps later instead of at 20.

Recommendation: option 3 short-term (one-line fix: \`usePatientList({ search, page_size: 100 })\`), then revisit pagination/infinite-scroll if any practice grows past 100.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A user with >20 patients can see them all in the UI
- [ ] Page shows the actual \`total\` somewhere so users know what they're looking at
- [ ] Tests cover the chosen page_size
close_reason: Patient list: page_size=100 + 'Showing N of M' total (y93); substring search across both names, search_by toggle dropped, generic placeholder (bgr). Closing with the PR.

title: Grant documentai.apiUser to prod backend SA
description:
## Problem

On 2026-05-24 we wired the Document AI OCR processor into Cloud Run for both pablohealth-dev and pablohealth-prod. Dev is fully functional. **Prod backend SA does not have \`roles/documentai.apiUser\`**, so when the OCR fallback fires it will get an auth-denied error from the Document AI API instead of successfully OCR'ing.

The Cloud Run env vars are already set on prod (revision pablo-backend-00249-qcp) — only the IAM grant is missing. Dev's backend SA already has this role, which is why dev works.

## Why this wasn't done automatically

Cross-environment IAM-modifying gcloud commands are blocked in the Claude Code harness on prod targets. The dev grant was done manually before the deploy; prod's was missed.

## The one-liner

\`\`\`bash
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding pablohealth-prod \\
  --member=serviceAccount:pablo-backend@pablohealth-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\
  --role=roles/documentai.apiUser \\
  --condition=None
\`\`\`

## Verify

After granting, upload a scanned PDF in prod and confirm the \"OCR not yet supported\" badge doesn't appear on the document row.

## Acceptance

- [ ] \`gcloud projects get-iam-policy pablohealth-prod\` shows pablo-backend SA with documentai.apiUser
- [ ] Scanned PDF upload in prod produces extracted_text (visible via patient document detail endpoint or chat citation manifest)
close_reason: IAM grant applied to pablohealth-prod by user; verified pablo-backend@pablohealth-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com now has roles/documentai.apiUser. Prod OCR fully wired.

title: Register intake/treatment_plan/safety_plan/medications note types in registry
description:
chat_context_bundler.py:79-82 references note-type keys for sources MOST_RECENT_INTAKE, TREATMENT_PLAN_ACTIVE, SAFETY_PLAN_ACTIVE, CURRENT_MEDICATIONS, but only 'soap' and 'narrative' are registered in backend/app/notes/registry.py (see docstring lines 25-31). Bundler defensively returns row_count=0 / reason=no_data for these.

Action: register the four types in the note-type registry so chat has clinical context beyond SOAP notes. Intake history and active treatment/safety plans + medication list materially change chat answers for prescriber and longitudinal-therapy workflows.

Coordinate with the chat-bundler patient_documents work so both land in the same chat-context iteration.
design:
CONTEXT (code-verified against main, 2026-08-17):

The chat context bundler already declares the note-type keys it looks for, and
they are not registered, so those sources are permanently empty:

  backend/app/services/chat_context_bundler.py
    SESSION_NOTE_TYPES        = {"soap", "narrative"}      <- registered
    INTAKE_NOTE_TYPES         = {"intake", "biopsychosocial"}
    TREATMENT_PLAN_NOTE_TYPES = {"treatment_plan"}
    SAFETY_PLAN_NOTE_TYPES    = {"safety_plan", "stanley_brown"}
    MEDICATIONS_NOTE_TYPES    = {"medications", "medication_list"}

Only `soap` and `narrative` exist, both in backend/app/notes/builtin.py, and
`register_builtin_note_types` (builtin.py:184-191) registers exactly those two
with `replace=True`. The bundler degrades quietly — `row_count=0`,
`reason=no_data` — so today chat answers a question about a patient's intake
history, active treatment or safety plan, or medication list with nothing at
all, and nothing anywhere reports that as a gap.

SCOPE: register the four missing note types as core definitions so those
sources can carry data.

THE FIELD THAT DECIDES CORRECTNESS: `NoteTypeDefinition.context`
(registry.py:101, `NoteContext = Literal["session", "patient", "practice"]`)
defaults to "session". The bundler splits on exactly this: session-context
notes feed `progress_notes_*`, patient-context notes feed the named sources.
All four of these are PATIENT-context — an intake, a treatment plan, a safety
plan and a medication list belong to the person, not to one appointment.
Registering them with the default would file them as progress notes and leave
the named sources just as empty as they are now, while looking like the work
was done. Set `context="patient"` on all four.

DEFINITIONS to add in backend/app/notes/builtin.py, following the shape of
NARRATIVE_DEFINITION (builtin.py:160) — key, label, description, tier="core",
context="patient", sections:

  - key "intake" — label "Intake". Sections should cover presenting concerns,
    history (psychiatric, medical, family, social), substance use, risk, and
    initial formulation.
  - key "treatment_plan" — label "Treatment Plan". Problems, goals, objectives,
    interventions, review date.
  - key "safety_plan" — label "Safety Plan". Follow the Stanley-Brown
    structure, since the bundler already recognises `stanley_brown` as an alias
    for this source: warning signs, internal coping strategies, people and
    social settings that distract, people to ask for help, professionals and
